paper_title: Thinking Fast, Anywhere: One System-1 for the Decision Points of Any Agent Workflow

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Autonomous LLM agents incur substantial cost and latency by invoking a large model (System-2) at every step, even when many intermediate actions choose among a small set of known candidates. Existing dual-system agents offload such decisions to a lightweight System-1 model, but rely on workflow-specific hooks authored per environment. We present AnyS1, a framework that turns human-authored procedural skills, whose instructions naturally specify where choices arise and which options apply, into a shared, domain-general source of decision points. Offline, AnyS1 mines grounded enumerable decisions across over 1,000 public skills, gathers execution-grounded trajectory states inside isolated containers to construct Any-DP, and trains a single calibrated 4B pointer System-1 with label smoothing. At run time, compiled workflows resolve routine decisions in one forward pass and fall back to System-2 when confidence falls below a calibrated threshold. Across three unseen benchmarks and distinct System-2 model families, AnyS1 preserves task reliability while cutting episode cost by 75-91% and model-call time by 63-92% relative to an uncompiled System-2 agent, and maintains performance under zero-shot threshold transfer.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Driven by advances in reasoning and tool use, large language models (LLMs) have evolved into autonomous agents capable of complex, long-horizon tasks (Kwa et al., 2025)resolving repositorylevel software issues (Yang et al., 2024), operating desktop and web interfaces (Xie et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2024), and handling policy-constrained customer workflows (Yao et al., 2025; Barres et al., 2025). Yet mainstream agent architectures invoke large model (System-2) at every step over growing trajectory (Yao et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2025), causing inference latency and cost to escalate rapidly (Kapoor et al., 2025)even though 1 many intermediate steps choose among small set of known options rather than requiring open-ended generation (4.4). Typed decision models offer fast alternative for such bounded choices (TypeSafe AI, 2026; Palmer, 2026): given the current state, question, and candidate options, they output an option distribution in single forward pass, acting as fast, intuitive System-1 alongside System-2 for planning, open generation, and uncertain fallbacks (Kahneman, 2011). While recent dual-system agents use this collaboration to substantially cut decision latency and cost in search and specialized tool harnesses (Cao et al., 2026; Zhu et al., 2026; Wu and Lim, 2026), they remain restricted to decision points manually pre-defined for single fixed workflow, collecting training supervision exclusively at those hard-coded hooks (Figure 1(a)). When general agent faces diverse tasks governed by new workflows without pre-declared hooks, every judgment falls back to System-2. We observe that general agents increasingly acquire workflows through agent skills (SKILL.md; Anthropic, 2025), paradigm uniting flexibility with procedurality. Across public repositories of over hundred thousand skills (FayeZC, 2026; Wang et al., 2026b), an agent can dynamically load relevant skills on demand, while each skill specifies structured procedure whose branches and checks implicitly define where to judge and among which options (Figure 1(b)). Procedural skills thus offer natural, workflow-agnostic source from which decision points can be mined automatically for dualsystem execution. Building on this insight, we propose AnyS1, framework that mines actionable decision points from procedural skills and extends single-LLM execution into calibrated dual-system collaboration (Figure 2). Offline, AnyS1 extracts verbatim-grounded enumerable decision points across over 1,000 public skills and executes synmarks, confirming that one skill-trained System1 generalizes across domains and System-2 families without retraining. Controlled analyses further show that training on authentic container-executed states outperforms LLM-fabricated states by +18.8 points on held-out observations, while calibration and confidence gating prevent cascading search failures and capture nearly the full savings ceiling set by each workflows enumerable-step share. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: (1) Skill-mined paradigm and dataset: we generalize dual-system agents from manually hardcoded workflow hooks to decision points mined automatically from procedural skills, releasing AnyDP across 1,072 public skills; (2) Calibrated dualsystem framework: we propose AnyS1, pairing one label-smoothed 4B System-1 pointer model with confidence deferral under zero-shot transfer (AnyS1cold) or unlabeled development calibration (AnyS1warm); (3) End-to-end validation and analysis: across three unseen benchmarks and two System-2 families, we demonstrate substantial cost and latency reductions at preserved success, establish why authentic execution states and calibration are essential, and characterize the enumerable-cost ceiling.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Agent skills and workflow compilation. Agent skills package procedural knowledge as instructions and resources loaded on demand without weight updates (Anthropic, 2025), extending executable skill libraries learned in open-ended play (Wang et al., 2024). One line of work studies how agents retrieve, follow and internalize skills (Xia et al., 2026; Lu et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026a; Dong et al., 2026; Cho and Park, 2026), or synthesizes interaction trajectories and verifiable tasks from skill corpora to fine-tune generative policies (Zeng et al., 2024; Song et al., 2024; Tan et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026a,b); complementary line compiles natural-language procedures into explicit programs (Khattab et al., 2024), turning SOPs into executable pseudo-code (Yu et al., 2026), skills into runtime interfaces or state machines (Chen et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2026a; Li, 2026), and recurring paths into scheduled workflows, deterministic rules or neurosymbolic programs (Xiang et al., 2026; Weber and Taneja, 2026; Liu et al., 2026; Suh et al., 2026; Mazza and Levi, 2026; Wang and Zang, 2026). However, prior skill-learning methods treat each Figure 1: Prior dual-system agents versus AnyS1. (a) Each prior agent adapts System-1 to one fixed workflow: engineers hand-pick its decision points and train System-1 specialized to them. (b) AnyS1 mines decision points from public skills once, offline, and trains one general System-1; any agent that selects skill then executes it as dual-system workflow. thesized tasks in isolated containers to build AnyDP 17,865 typed decision points and 25,986 teacher-consensus execution statestraining one 4B System-1 pointer model with label smoothing for cross-workflow calibration. At run time, compiled workflows run deterministic steps as code, keep open generation on System-2, and score enumerable decisions with System-1 in one forward pass: confidence gate adopts millisecond System1 choices above threshold (calibrated on unlabeled development runs in AnyS1warm or transferred zero-shot in AnyS1cold) and defers uncertain cases to System-2. We evaluate AnyS1 end-to-end on three unseen agent benchmarksSOPBench, ALFWorld, and WebShopacross two distinct System-2 backbones (DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash and GPT-6 Sol). Relative to an uncompiled System-2 agent that reads skills directly, AnyS1warm resolves most enumerable decisions in single millisecond-scale pass, reducing episode cost by 7591% and cutting criticalpath model time by 6392% across both System-2 backbones without sacrificing task success. With zero target-workflow runs, directly transferring single global threshold (AnyS1cold) likewise preserves task reliability across all three unseen bench2 skill as unified prompt or trajectory-level target for single generative model, while compiled workflows still rely on LLM calls, static rules or uncalibrated heuristic guards at semantic branches. In contrast, AnyS1 operates at the granularity of individual decisions inside skills: we mine enumerable decision points across diverse skills and harvest real execution states (Any-DP) to train one calibrated System-1, turning compiled skill execution into collaborative System-1System-2 workflow. Typed decision models and calibrated deferral. Inspired by dual-process theory (Kahneman, 2011) and LLM cascades (Chen et al., 2024; Ong et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2026b), early fastslow agents pair small text generator or modular executor with slow planner (Lin et al., 2023; Yin et al., 2024; Prasad et al., 2024; Saha et al., 2025; Su et al., 2025), whereas typed decision models cast System1 as non-generative scorer returning option probabilities in one forward pass. Following commercial Jev (TypeSafe AI, 2026), open-weight models either attach pointer or decision heads to open LMsfor general choices (Kev; Palmer, 2026) or domain-specific agent states (SearchJev, Cao et al., 2026; AgentDecision, Zhu et al., 2026)or read debiased probabilities via cyclic permutations (AnyJev; Zhang et al., 2026) to mitigate order sensitivity (Zheng et al., 2024). Dual-system agents built on these models accelerate search (Cao et al., 2026) and tool use (Wu and Lim, 2026; Zhu et al., 2026) via selective deferral to an LLM (Geifman and El-Yaniv, 2017; Sowietzki et al., 2026; Hemadri et al., 2026), with recent studies analyzing delegation boundaries and biases (Vats, 2026; Li et al., 2026b; Lukassen et al., 2026; Sun et al., 2026). We generalize this paradigm beyond per-workflow manual hooks by mining decision points from skills and serving them with one label-smoothed System1 (Guo et al., 2017; Müller et al., 2019) under unlabeled development calibration (AnyS1warm) or zero-shot transfer (AnyS1cold).

sections.title: 3.1 Problem Formulation
sections.content: From singleto dual-system execution. Consider an agent executing task by following skill over multi-step episode: at each step t, the agent observes the current state st (accumulated context, tool outputs and user messages) and produces an action or decision. conventional single-system agent queries the LLM (System-2) at every step to reason and generate the output. To turn this into dual-system execution, we draw on dual-process theory (Kahneman, 2011) and classify workflow steps by task type and decision complexity into three node types: node (deterministic) is fully determined by structured state (e.g., fixed tool call) and runs directly as code; node (generative) produces open-ended output and stays with System-2; and an node (enumerable) reads unstructured content in state and selects one option from finite candidate set fixed in the skill or listable from s, making it suited to System-1 delegation. We formalize each skill-specified node as decision point template (q, O, d): question q, options = {o1, . . . , on} with one-sentence definitions d(o), and none of the above; triggered at state s, it forms runtime instance = (s, q, O, d). System-1 and delegation. sections.title: 3.2 Skill-Grounded Data Synthesis: Any-DP
sections.content: To train general System-1, we construct Any-DP by first mining decision point templates (q, O, d) from unstructured skill prose (SKILL.md) and then executing synthesized tasks in isolated containers to collect authentic runtime states and consensus labels O. Extracting decision points from skills. To ensure that mined decision points reflect genuine workflow branches, for each skill an LLM analyzer independently reads SKILL.md and its bundled documents three times, returning typed candidate decision points with options and verbatim supporting quote verified via exact string matching against the skill text. We then call an LLM to merge equivalent points across the three runs, record support σ(p) {1, 2, 3}, take the majority value per field, and write one-sentence option definition d(o) from the skill text to disambiguate identically named options. We retain nodes with σ(p) 2 that are answerable from state alone, yielding grounded templates (q, O, d). Synthesizing executable tasks from skills. Extracted templates (q, O, d) specify what to judge, yet training System-1 also requires states that reflect genuine runtime contexts: asking an LLM to fabricate states directly yields clean prose summaries that fail to generalize to fragmented tool outputs along real trajectories. To automatically elicit authentic deep-branch states across diverse skills, for each skill (split beforehand at the repository level into training and held-out sets to prevent leakage) an LLM synthesizes self-contained multi-stage tasks complete with input files, reference solution, and hidden verifier, paired with two cross-category distractor skills that require the agent to both select the right skill and advance across dependent stages; task is retained only if, inside network-isolated container, the verifier rejects the initial files and accepts the reference solution. Trajectory execution and state labeling. To capture authentic interaction contexts, we use an OpenHands agent (Wang et al., 2025) to execute each verified task in the isolated container, after which an LLM locator aligns the trajectory to the skills decision points and extracts verbatim the preceding observations (task instructions, user messages, and raw tool outputs) at the step where each decision arises. Synthesized dataset Any-DP. Running this pipeline on 1,072 public skills from SkillMD-138K (FayeZC, 2026)spanning 16 categories such as web front-end, software engineering, and data analysisyields Any-DP, comprising 17,865 typed decision points, 2,846 container-verified tasks, and 25,986 consensus-labeled examples  (Table 1)  . Its distribution highlights two key properties: first, enumerable nodes account for 64.5% of all workflow nodes and 100% of skills contain at least one node, showing that bounded decisions are pervasive across procedural skills; second, 64.6% of nodes require contextual semantic inference rather than literal lookup (17.8%), underscoring why static rules cannot replace learned System-1. Moreover, dual-teacher consensus reaches 89.2%, with strict repository-level exclusion of all evaluation-related skills (Appendix A).

sections.title: 4 Experiments
sections.content: We evaluate AnyS1 around four research questions. RQ1: Does AnyS1 cut cost and latency on unseen workflows without lowering task success? RQ2: How do the gate, executed states, and calibrated loss each contribute? RQ3: What governs the savings? RQ4: Does calibrated confidence select the right decisions to delegate?

sections.title: 4.1 Experimental Setup
sections.content: Benchmarks. To test cross-domain generalization without retraining, we evaluate on three unseen agent benchmarks spanning policy-constrained dialogue, partially observable embodied search, and noisy web navigation, with zero skill overlap with 5 Any-DP (Appendices and B): (1) SOPBench (Li et al., 2026c) evaluates multi-turn customer-service dialogues under strict procedural and database constraints across 268 held-out tasks, compiled deterministically from machine-readable SOPs; (2) ALFWorld (Shridhar et al., 2021) tests multi-room object search and manipulation across 134 unseen text-based household tasks, compiled from SkillRL skill banks (Xia et al., 2026) into six task-family programs; and (3) WebShop (Yao et al., 2022) evaluates goal-directed shopping over 1.18M-product web catalog across 500 user instructions (search formulation, attribute/price checks, and option selection within 15 steps), compiled from SkillRL skills into seven category programs. Models and configurations. We pair single 4B System-1 trained exclusively on Any-DP with DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash as the primary System-2 and GPT-6 Sol as cross-family System-2 (decoding settings in Appendix B). We compare three baselines(i) an uncompiled System-2 agent with skills reading raw skill documents directly (the SOPBench reference agent; ReAct with SkillRL skills on ALFWorld and WebShop); (ii) Compiled workflow (All-S2), where System-2 executes every and node; and (iii) commercial Jev as System1 (jev-1.14.0; TypeSafe AI, 2026)against two AnyS1 variants: AnyS1warm, whose scalar threshold τ is calibrated on 50 unlabeled development runs per benchmark (3.3), and cold-start AnyS1cold, which transfers single threshold (τ = 0.918) with zero target-workflow runs. When switching System-2 to GPT-6 Sol, System-1 and AnyS1cold remain completely unchanged while AnyS1warm refits only τ on 50 unlabeled Sol development episodes; component ablations such as removing the gate (All-S1) are analyzed in 4.3. Metrics and protocol. For task effectiveness, we report Pass (%) on SOPBench (tasks satisfying all final dialogue and database constraints), Success Rate (SR) (%) on ALFWorld, and both continuous Score (0100) and binary exact-match SR (%) on WebShop. For efficiency, following Zhu et al. (2026), we report per-episode cost savings relative to the uncompiled System-2 agent with skills under the same System-2 (Sav. %; pricing System-2 and commercial Jev at official API list rates$0.042/1M input tokens and $0 output for Jevand our open-weight 4B System-1 by selfhosted L4 GPU serving throughput at $0.0045 per 1K single-pass decisions) alongside mean criticalpath model-call time per episode (Time (s)). All thresholds were pre-registered before test runs, and each configuration shares an exact System-2 request cache with All-S2 so runs diverge strictly where System-1 answers.

sections.title: 4.2 RQ1: Main Results
sections.content: Skill compilation and calibrated delegation provide complementary efficiency gains. Table 2 separates two orthogonal levers behind end-to-end efficiency. First, compiling unstructured skills into explicit D/E/G workflows (All-S2) removes mechanical tool orchestration from LLM turns and arrests prompt accumulation across dialogue history, preventing step-skipping, lifting macro-average effectiveness by nearly 18 points, and saving 7686% of the uncompiled agents episode cost (81% on average). Second, offloading routine decisions to single-pass System-1 under AnyS1warm raises the average saving to 89% (8691% across benchmarks) and cuts critical-path model time by 70 92% relative to the uncompiled agent (vs. 5187% for All-S2), while matching All-S2 reliability on average (+0.5 avg. pt). In fact, single-pass local scoring suppresses verbose System-2 over-deliberation on straightforward binary relevance checks, improving WebShop score over All-S2 (68.1 vs. 66.9). Compared against commercial Jev, self-hosted 4B AnyS1 saves more of the uncompiled agents cost (89% vs. 84% on average) at lower per-episode latency by avoiding remote API round-trips. Even without target-workflow runs, cold-start AnyS1cold stays level with All-S2 (+0.1 avg. pt) while saving 87% of the uncompiled agents cost on average. single System-1 generalizes across System2 model families without retraining. sections.title: 4.3 RQ2: Component Ablation Study
sections.content: To isolate the role of each component, Table 3 evaluates ablations along three dimensions: (a) runtime deferral gating, (b) training state source, and (c) calibration objective (detailed setups in Appendix B). Confidence gating prevents cascading search failures in long horizons. Comparing our calibrated gates (AnyS1warm and AnyS1cold) against ungated All-S1which delegates every decision to System-1 unconditionallyshows that shorthorizon routing workflows remain intact without gating, whereas long-horizon ALFWorld exploration collapses (96.3% 40.3%). Both AnyS1warm and AnyS1cold intercept uncertain openended exploration states via calibrated ranking rather than lower delegation volumeequal-rate random delegation multiplies System-2 disagreements more than fourfold (Appendix C). Container-executed states bridge the observation gap left by synthetic summaries. We compare Any-DP against LLM-written synthetic (S1-syn), which trains the same 4B architecture on LLM-drafted state summaries conditioned on mined decision points without container execution. Training on Any-DPs executed container states outperforms S1-syn across every splitmost notably by +18.8 points on the held-out container development set (Dev) and +5.3 points on ALFWorld Eplausibly because idealized synthetic summaries mismatch terse, truncated terminal outputs. Label smoothing prevents out-of-domain confidence saturation. Replacing Eq. 3 with unsmoothed hard-label cross-entropy or CE + Brier on the same Any-DP training set yields nearly unchanged raw accuracy yet degrades out-of-domain calibration (Table 3c). Because unsmoothed logits saturate near probability 1.0 even on unfamiliar states, the dev-fitted threshold inflates toward τ = 0.998 and degrades cross-domain gated agreement (mean agreement drops from 97.7% to 92.4 93.7%), whereas label smoothing preserves uniform probability mass and transferable confidence margin (Appendix C). sections.title: 4.4 RQ3: What Governs the Savings?
sections.content: Workflow E-node share governs both cost and latency ceilings. Normalizing episode cost and time to the uncompiled agent via Eq. 1 (Figure 3) shows that post-compilation delegation targets the remaining share: nodes hold 1722% of uncompiled cost and 1118% of time on ALFWorld and WebShop, vs. 4% and 19% on SOPBench (G nodes: 10% and 30%). Delegating nearly all SOPBench nodes under AnyS1warm approaches this bound, plus residual G-node drop (9.9% to 8.8%). Single-pass scoring converts delegation into critical-path speedup. Locally served System1 scores all options in 21.831.7 ms median (Appendix B), 5681 faster than 1.511.78 System2 calls. sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: We presented AnyS1, turning on-demand procedural skills into shared source of structured decision points without custom per-workflow System1 engineering. By mining grounded enumerable judgments across public skills, collecting containerexecuted states, and training one label-smoothed pointer System-1, AnyS1 resolves routine steps and calibrates deferral to System-2 in one forward pass. Experiments across unseen benchmarks and distinct System-2 model families show that both unlabeled calibration and zero-shot threshold transfer preserve all-System-2 reliability at substantially lower cost and critical-path latency.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: While AnyS1cold transfers with zero targetworkflow executions, achieving the largest cost reductions under AnyS1warm uses about 50 development episodes per workflow in which System-2 answers every node, and large episode-level cost savings rely on compiling procedural skills into explicit programs; adapting deferral thresholds online from deferred System-2 calls and automatically compiling open-ended repository skills are natural next steps.

sections.title: Worked Example
sections.content: Source curation and split isolation. We curate procedural skills from SkillMD-138K (FayeZC, 2026) according to four criteria: (i) procedural structure and licensing, retaining multi-step English procedural documents released under permissive open-source SPDX licenses while excluding bulk aggregator repositories; (ii) diversity and deduplication, applying MinHash near-duplicate removal and capping at most three skills per repository so no single codebase dominates; (iii) split isolation and benchmark decontamination, partitioning repositories into disjoint training and held-out sets beforehand and excluding any skill that references downstream evaluation or public containerized agent benchmarks (SOPBench, ALFWorld, WebShop, SkillRL, or τ -bench); and (iv) sandbox executability, verifying that each skill can run endto-end inside an offline Linux container without external accounts or live human input. Stratified sampling across 16 functional categories yields the 1,072 public training skills in Any-DP. Decision-point filtering and task synthesis. Across three extraction passes per skill (Figure 5, Prompt 1), an LLM merger retains nodes with support σ(p) 2 that express non-preference judgments, are answerable from local text context, and include at least two candidate options alongside none of the above. For skills with at least three retained nodes, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash generates multi-stage Linux tasks paired with crosscategory distractors, hidden verifier, and reference solution that passes inside an isolated container (Prompt 2). summary. Execution labeling and dataset OpenHands agents (Wang et al., 2025) execute the verified tasks, trajectory locator copies verbatim pre-decision observations (user messages and tool outputs, excluding agent reasoning), and two orderreversed teacher passes assign consensus labels (Prompt 3). Overall, 2,846 verified tasks across 1,072 skills yield 17,865 mined decision points and 25,986 consensus examples (89.2% teacher agreement; median 3 options besides none of the above; 6.7% labeled none of the above). Applying the same labeling protocol to disjoint Apache2.0 containerized trajectories gives the 153 calibration states (AnyS1cold) and 185 offline development states (Dev, Appendix C). sections.content: Full offline baseline comparison. Expanding Table 3(b), Table 4 evaluates System-1 (three seeds) across our offline development sets (Dev, SOPBench E, ALFWorld E, and its search subset) against zero-shot typed decision models (Kev4B, AgentDecision-4B, commercial Jev), zeroshot Qwen3.5-4B/27B, and S1-syn. On heldout Dev, System-1 (83.8%) outperforms S1-syn (65.0%) and commercial Jev (78.4%), while the option-interaction head improves over standard pointer head (82.7%) by +1.1 points; on ALFWorld search, the stronger 4B models (Qwen3.54B, AgentDecision-4B, and both Any-DP heads) plateau at 3844% due to missing room priors.
